2.1.1:
Why this matters

When a problem appears, people jump to the first cause that comes to mind, usually something that confirms what they already believed. A fishbone diagram forces the team to list all the possible causes, in an organized way, before anyone decides which is the real one. It is the main brainstorming tool of Six Sigma.

The big idea

The cause-and-effect diagram, invented by Kaoru Ishikawa (so also called the Ishikawa diagram), looks like the skeleton of a fish:

  • The head is the effect: the problem, stated as a measurable outcome.
  • The spine runs back from the head.
  • The bones are categories of causes.
  • Smaller bones on each bone are specific possible causes, and sub-causes branch off those.

Each bone is a category; each small line is a possible cause the team suspects.

The standard categories

For manufacturing and operations, the 6M categories are the usual starting point:

  1. Man (people): skills, training, fatigue, staffing.
  2. Machine: equipment, tools, trucks, software.
  3. Method: procedures, work instructions, routes, scheduling.
  4. Material: raw materials, parts, freight, information inputs.
  5. Measurement: gauges, data accuracy, how results are recorded.
  6. Mother Nature (environment): weather, temperature, humidity, traffic, lighting.

For service and transactional processes, 4P or 8P lists often fit better: People, Process, Policies, Procedures, and for marketing-type problems Place, Product, Price, Promotion. The categories are only prompts. Use whatever set helps the team think broadly; you can invent your own ("Customers", "Systems").

How to build one

  1. Write the effect at the head as a specific, measurable problem: "Late deliveries in the Southeast region", not "bad service".
  2. Draw the main bones with the chosen categories.
  3. Brainstorm causes with people who know the process. For each idea, ask "which category?" and add it to that bone.
  4. Drill down by asking "why does that happen?" and adding sub-causes. The 5 Whys technique asks "why?" repeatedly (roughly five times) until you reach a cause you can act on:
  • Late delivery. Why? Truck left late. Why? Loading finished late. Why? Freight arrived late at the dock. Why? Picking started late. Why? Pick lists print only after the 6 a.m. batch run.
  1. Mark the suspects: the team votes or uses experience to circle the most likely causes for data checking.

What the fishbone does not do

A fishbone diagram is a list of hypotheses. It does not prove any cause. "The fishbone identified the root cause" is false: it identified possible causes. Proving which ones matter is the job of data in the Measure and Analyze phases (C&E matrix, data collection, hypothesis tests, regression).

Where its output goes

The candidate causes from the fishbone feed the C&E (X-Y) matrix (2.1.3), which ranks them, and the top-ranked ones go into the data collection plan and are tested statistically in Analyze.

Worked example

Effect: "Invoices sent with wrong amounts: 6% of invoices". A billing team lists:

  • People: new clerks, unclear who checks.
  • Method: rates keyed by hand, no second check, accessorial charges added after.
  • Machine (systems): rate table not updated automatically, two systems not linked.
  • Material (inputs): delivery paperwork missing charges, illegible bills of lading.
  • Measurement: error counted only when the customer complains.
  • Environment: month-end rush.

The team circles three suspects (manual rate entry, late accessorials, rate table updates) and plans to collect data on each invoice error's cause for four weeks.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • A fishbone generates hypotheses, it does not prove causes.
  • A vague effect gives vague causes. Make the head specific and measurable.
  • Listing solutions instead of causes ("buy new software") on the bones.
  • 6M names: Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature.

Check yourself

  1. What goes at the head of the fishbone?
  2. Name the 6M categories.
  3. True or false: a completed fishbone diagram identifies the root cause.
  4. What technique drills down from a cause to a deeper cause by repeatedly asking a question?
  5. Where do the fishbone's causes go next in DMAIC?
Show answers
  1. The effect, the specific measurable problem.
  2. Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature (environment).
  3. False. It lists possible causes; data must confirm them.
  4. The 5 Whys.
  5. Into the C&E matrix for ranking, then into data collection and statistical testing in Analyze.

Key takeaways

  • Effect at the head; categories as bones; causes and sub-causes as smaller bones.
  • 6M for operations; 4P/8P for services; categories are prompts.
  • Use 5 Whys to drill down.
  • It produces hypotheses, not proof; feed them into the C&E matrix and test with data.
2.1.2:
Why this matters

People who work in a process usually disagree about how it actually works. Drawing it out, together, reveals handoffs, loops, waiting and duplicated work that nobody could see. Process maps are the most-used Measure tools after data collection itself.

The big idea

There are maps at different levels of detail, for different purposes:

  1. SIPOC: one-page, high-level view, used in Define to agree on scope.
  2. Flowchart / process map: step-by-step detail, including decisions and loops.
  3. Swimlane map: a flowchart divided by who does each step, to show handoffs.
  4. Value stream map (VSM): the Lean map, adding time, inventory and information flow, to show where lead time goes.

SIPOC

SIPOC stands for Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers. It is a table that describes the process at the highest level:

SuppliersInputsProcessOutputsCustomers
ShipperOrder, freight1. Receive orderDelivered freightConsignee
DispatchLoad plan2. Plan loadSigned receiptShipper
FleetTruck, driver3. Pick upInvoiceBilling
Fuel vendorFuel4. Transport
5. Deliver

Rules:

  • The process column has only 4 to 7 high-level steps. Any more and it is not high-level.
  • Building it usually starts in the middle (the process), then outputs and customers, then inputs and suppliers.
  • It sets the start and stop points (scope) and shows everyone involved.

Flowcharts and their symbols

The basic symbols. Most maps need only these.

  • Terminator (rounded rectangle, or oval): start or end.
  • Process (rectangle): a step where something is done.
  • Decision (diamond): a question with branches (yes/no, pass/fail).
  • Document (wavy bottom): a form, report or paperwork.
  • Arrows: the order and direction of flow.

Some maps also use a circle (connector to another page), a delay symbol (D-shape) and an inventory triangle.

Swimlane maps

A swimlane (cross-functional) map puts each person, department or system in its own horizontal or vertical lane. Every time the flow crosses a lane boundary, that is a handoff. Handoffs are where delays and errors gather: information gets lost, work waits in an inbox, responsibility is unclear. Counting lane crossings is often a quick way to find improvement opportunities.

Levels and states

  • Start with a high-level map (SIPOC level), then a detailed map of the area in scope. For each step, you can list its inputs and outputs, which later feed the C&E matrix.
  • As-is (current state) maps show how the work really happens today, including rework loops and workarounds. Map what people actually do, not what the procedure says. Walk the process (a gemba walk) instead of mapping from a conference room.
  • To-be (future state) maps show the improved design, used in Improve.

A spaghetti diagram traces the physical path of a person or item across a floor plan. The tangled lines show wasted motion and conveyance at a glance.

Value stream maps

A value stream map follows one product or service family from request to delivery and adds data:

  • Process boxes with a data box below: cycle time (C/T), changeover time (C/O), uptime, number of operators, batch size.
  • Inventory triangles between steps, with the quantity waiting or the waiting time.
  • Push arrows (striped) where work is pushed, pull/kanban symbols where it is pulled.
  • Information flow at the top: how orders and schedules move (electronic, paper, verbal).
  • A timeline ladder at the bottom: the upper steps show waiting time, the lower steps show value-added (processing) time.

Most of the 4-day lead time is waiting in front of steps; only 75 minutes is processing.

Reading a VSM: lead time, VA time and PCE

From the timeline:

  • Total lead time = sum of the waiting times + sum of the processing times. Here: 2.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 days = 4.0 days, plus 75 minutes.
  • Total value-added time = sum of the processing (cycle) times that add value: 20 + 15 + 40 = 75 minutes.
  • Process cycle efficiency (PCE) = VA time ÷ lead time = 75 min ÷ (4 × 1,440 min) ≈ 1.3%.

The largest non-value-added delay is the biggest waiting segment (2 days before Receive): the first target.

Bottlenecks and capacity

The bottleneck is the step with the longest cycle time (or lowest capacity). It limits the output of the whole process: nothing can come out faster than the bottleneck can work.

In the map above, Load (40 min) is the bottleneck. In an 8-hour shift (480 min) it can load 480 ÷ 40 = 12 trailers, so the process makes at most 12 a shift, however fast Receive and Sort are. Compare with takt time (1.2.5): if customers need 16 trailers a shift, takt = 480 ÷ 16 = 30 min, and Load at 40 min cannot keep up.

Improving any step other than the bottleneck does not increase output; it just grows the pile in front of the bottleneck.

Worked example

A VSM shows: Order entry (C/T 5 min), wait 3 days, Credit check (C/T 10 min), wait 1 day, Scheduling (C/T 15 min), wait 2 days, Dispatch (C/T 10 min).

  1. VA time = 5 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 40 min.
  2. Lead time ≈ 6 days (8,640 min) + 40 min ≈ 8,680 min.
  3. PCE = 40 ÷ 8,680 ≈ 0.46%.
  4. Largest delay: 3 days between order entry and credit check.
  5. Bottleneck by cycle time: scheduling (15 min).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • SIPOC has 4 to 7 high-level steps. It is not a detailed map.
  • Map the as-is truthfully, including rework and workarounds.
  • PCE = VA time ÷ total lead time, not ÷ processing time.
  • The bottleneck is the longest cycle time, not the longest wait.
  • Handoffs show up in swimlanes as lane crossings.

Check yourself

  1. What do the letters in SIPOC stand for?
  2. Which flowchart symbol is a diamond?
  3. On a VSM, what do the upper and lower steps of the timeline ladder show?
  4. Steps have cycle times of 12, 18 and 9 minutes. Which is the bottleneck, and how many units can the process make in 360 minutes?
  5. VA time 30 min, lead time 2 days. What is PCE?
Show answers
  1. Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers.
  2. A decision.
  3. Upper: waiting (non-value-added) time. Lower: processing (value-added) time.
  4. The 18-minute step; 360 ÷ 18 = 20 units.
  5. 30 ÷ 2,880 ≈ 1.0%.

Key takeaways

  • SIPOC: one page, 4 to 7 steps, defines scope.
  • Flowcharts: terminator, process, decision, document, arrows. Swimlanes show handoffs.
  • Map the as-is honestly (walk the gemba); design the to-be in Improve.
  • VSM adds cycle times, inventory, information flow and a timeline ladder.
  • PCE = VA time ÷ lead time; bottleneck = longest cycle time, it sets the process's output.
2.1.3:
Why this matters

A fishbone can produce 40 possible causes, and there is not enough time to collect data on all of them. The C&E matrix is a quick, structured way to rank them by how much they are believed to affect what the customer cares about, so data collection focuses on the most likely few.

The big idea

The cause-and-effect matrix (also X-Y matrix or XY diagram) is a table:

  • Columns: the important outputs (Y's, usually the CTQs), each with an importance weight (often 1 to 10), from the customer's point of view.
  • Rows: the process inputs (X's), from the fishbone and process map.
  • Cells: the team rates how strongly each X affects each Y, usually with 0, 1, 3, 9: 0 = no relationship, 1 = weak, 3 = moderate, 9 = strong. The big jump to 9 spreads the scores so strong relationships stand out.
  • Row total for each X: multiply each rating by its column's importance and add across the row.
Score for an X = Σ (importance of Y × rating of X on that Y)

Sort the X's by score. The top few are the ones to measure and test first.

Worked example

Outputs: on-time delivery (importance 10), no damage (8), correct invoice (5).

Input (X)On-time (10)No damage (8)Invoice (5)Score
Loading method3903×10 + 9×8 + 0×5 = 102
Dispatch timing91090 + 8 + 0 = 98
Rate table accuracy0090 + 0 + 45 = 45
Driver experience33130 + 24 + 5 = 59

Ranked: loading method (102), dispatch timing (98), driver experience (59), rate table (45). The team collects data on loading method and dispatch timing first.

What it is and is not

  • It is a prioritization tool based on team judgment. The ratings are opinions from people who know the process.
  • It is not proof. A high score means "worth testing", not "is the cause". The top X's must be validated with data in Analyze.
  • It is only as good as the people in the room. Include operators, not just managers.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting the importance weights: multiply each rating by the Y's importance before adding.
  • Using 1 to 5 ratings when the question says 0/1/3/9.
  • Treating the ranking as validated: it still needs data.

Check yourself

  1. What are the rows and columns of a C&E matrix?
  2. Why use 0, 1, 3, 9 instead of 0, 1, 2, 3?
  3. Y importances are 10 and 4. An X is rated 9 and 3. What is its score?
  4. Does the top-scoring X have to be a root cause?
  5. Which earlier tools feed the list of X's?
Show answers
  1. Rows: inputs (X's). Columns: outputs (Y's) with importance weights.
  2. To spread scores apart so strong relationships stand out.
  3. 9 × 10 + 3 × 4 = 102.
  4. No. It is a judgment-based priority that must be confirmed with data.
  5. The fishbone diagram and the process map (inputs per step).

Key takeaways

  • Rank X's by their judged effect on weighted Y's.
  • Ratings 0/1/3/9; score = Σ importance × rating.
  • Top X's go into data collection; they are hypotheses until validated.
2.1.4:
Why this matters

Most improvement tools react to problems that already happened. FMEA looks ahead: what could go wrong, how bad would it be, how likely is it, and would we catch it? It lets a team prevent failures, especially severe ones, before customers are hurt.

The big idea

For each step of a process (or each part of a design), the team asks:

  1. How could this step fail? (failure mode)
  2. If it failed, what would happen? (effect) How bad? (severity)
  3. What would cause it? How often? (occurrence)
  4. What do we already do to prevent or catch it? (current controls) How likely would we catch it before the customer? (detection)

Each answer gets a rating from 1 to 10, and the ratings combine into a priority.

The FMEA columns

ColumnMeaning
Process stepWhere in the process
Failure modeHow the step could fail (load not secured)
EffectWhat the customer or next step experiences (freight shifts, damage)
Severity (S)How serious the effect is, 1 to 10
CauseWhy the failure would happen (straps worn, no checklist)
Occurrence (O)How often the cause happens, 1 to 10
Current controlsExisting prevention or detection (supervisor spot check)
Detection (D)How likely the failure escapes, 1 to 10
RPNS × O × D
Recommended action, owner, dateWhat to do about it
New S, O, D, RPNRatings after the action

The rating scales

Each organization writes its own descriptions, but the direction is standard:

  • Severity: 10 = most severe (hazardous, safety or legal), 1 = no noticeable effect.
  • Occurrence: 10 = very frequent (almost certain), 1 = extremely unlikely.
  • Detection: reverse scale. 10 = cannot detect (the failure will almost certainly reach the customer), 1 = almost certain to be detected.

Detection catches people out: a high detection number is bad.

Risk priority number (RPN)

RPN = S × O × D

Since each rating is 1 to 10, RPN ranges from 1 to 1,000. Higher RPN = higher priority for action.

Severity first

RPN treats the three ratings as equally important, which can hide danger. A failure mode with S = 10, O = 2, D = 3 has RPN = 60, lower than a nuisance with S = 4, O = 5, D = 5 (RPN = 100). But a severity 10 (for example, an injury) deserves attention regardless of RPN. Standard practice: any high-severity failure mode (9 or 10) gets reviewed and acted on first, whatever its RPN.

The current AIAG-VDA FMEA Handbook (2019), used in the automotive industry, replaced RPN with Action Priority (AP): a lookup table that rates each S-O-D combination High, Medium or Low priority, weighting severity first, then occurrence, then detection. The handbook says RPN thresholds are not a recommended way to decide on actions. For the IASSC exam, know RPN = S × O × D and the severity-first rule, and recognize AP as the newer method.

Reducing risk

  • Severity usually changes only if the design changes (the effect itself becomes less serious).
  • Occurrence falls when you remove or reduce the cause: mistake-proofing, better materials, training.
  • Detection improves when you add or strengthen controls that catch the failure before it reaches the customer.

Prevention (lowering occurrence) is better than detection, for the same reason as in COPQ (1.2.3). After actions, the team re-rates S, O and D and recomputes RPN to show the risk reduction.

Types and timing

  • DFMEA (design FMEA): failure modes of a product design.
  • PFMEA (process FMEA): failure modes of a process. Green Belt projects mostly use PFMEA.
  • An FMEA is a living document: started in Measure (to help find risks and causes), updated in Improve (to assess the risks of the new process), and kept current in Control.

Worked example

Failure modeSODRPN
A: Load not secured, freight shifts846192
B: Wrong delivery address on paperwork56390
C: Reefer temperature alarm ignored, product spoils1025100
D: Delivery receipt not scanned37484

By RPN alone, the order is A (192), C (100), B (90), D (84). But C has severity 10 (a spoiled food load can be a safety and legal problem), so it gets action alongside A, even though its RPN is lower than A's.

After installing a reefer alarm that auto-alerts dispatch, C's detection drops from 5 to 2: new RPN = 10 × 2 × 2 = 40. Severity stays 10, because a spoiled load is still just as bad if it happens.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Detection is reverse-scaled: 10 = hardest to detect.
  • Do not pick by RPN alone: check severity first.
  • Severity does not drop because of better detection; only design changes reduce severity.
  • Re-score after actions: the FMEA should show before and after.
  • RPN range is 1 to 1,000.

Check yourself

  1. What does each letter in S, O, D stand for, and which scale is reversed?
  2. Calculate RPN for S = 7, O = 3, D = 8.
  3. Failure mode X: S 9, O 2, D 4. Failure mode Y: S 5, O 6, D 5. Which do you address first, and why?
  4. A new inspection camera is added. Which rating should improve?
  5. In which DMAIC phases is the FMEA used?
Show answers
  1. Severity, occurrence, detection. Detection is reversed: 10 means least likely to be detected.
  2. 7 × 3 × 8 = 168.
  3. RPNs: X = 72, Y = 150. By RPN, Y is higher, but X has severity 9, so X should be reviewed and actioned first (or at least alongside Y).
  4. Detection.
  5. Measure (identify risks and causes), Improve (assess the new process), Control (keep it current).

Key takeaways

  • FMEA asks what could fail, how bad, how often, and would we catch it.
  • RPN = S × O × D, from 1 to 1,000; detection is reverse-scaled.
  • High severity gets action regardless of RPN; newer AIAG-VDA practice uses Action Priority.
  • Reduce occurrence (prevent) before improving detection; re-score after actions.
  • DFMEA = design, PFMEA = process; a living document.
